Tutorial

This page is a guided Angular tutorial for building one complete feature with from the ground up. You will move step by step from project setup, to Feature State definition, to registration and initialization, and finally to a working UI that reads, selects, creates, updates, deletes, filters, and derives managed State.

By the end of the page, you will have a typed , an Angular service that owns the Feature boundary, a component that binds to reactive State, and a complete character workflow that can render, select, create, update, delete, filter, sort, and derive display-ready values from a managed collection.

Business Use Case
  • A product team needs a simple detail view that presents one record from a managed collection without exposing state-management mechanics in the component.
  • The feature must keep domain ownership in a service so UI code can stay focused on display logic, template binding, and user interaction.
  • The same structure should scale from a read-only detail screen to later workflows such as editing, validation, loading states, and testing without changing the core boundary.

Chapter 1

Foundation Flow

The first tutorial builds the SDuX foundation from the first file onward: project setup, feature contract definition, registration, service ownership, and the first managed read path.

This chapter stays focused on one controlled outcome: a service-owned that can expose committed State to the UI without pushing state-management mechanics into the component.

Chapter 2

Multi-Select Flow

This chapter turns a fixed read view into a user-selected read path. The same service-owned now exposes a managed collection that the component can present through a dropdown-driven selection flow.

The important shift is architectural, not mechanical: selection stays local to the component, while Feature State remains owned by the service. The result is a more interactive read experience without moving State ownership out of the existing boundary.

Chapter 3

Add/Edit Flow

This chapter introduces mutation by adding merge configuration, create behavior, and update behavior to the same boundary. The workflow expands from reading data to saving new and edited records through the service.

Keep mutation policy inside the pipeline and committed Feature State inside the service, while the component owns only local form, mode, and feedback state. That separation makes the add/edit flow extensible instead of ad hoc.

Chapter 4

Delete Flow

This chapter adds delete behavior without moving collection ownership, delete rules, or confirmation logic into the template. The workflow now supports destructive updates through the same service-owned boundary.

Keep the same split in place: the service is still the only place that updates committed Feature State, while the component owns local selection, confirmation, editor, and feedback state. Keeping that line clear makes delete behavior easier to follow and easier to maintain.

Chapter 5

Lifecycle Flow

This chapter shifts from record mutation to lifecycle control by distinguishing persisted null, runtime reset, and permanent destruction of the .

The service still owns every lifecycle API, while the component responds by clearing or disabling local UI state. That separation makes it clear why replaceState({{ '{' }} value: null {{ '}' }}), reset(), and destroy() are related but not interchangeable.

Chapter 6

Filters and Reducers Flow

This chapter focuses on pipeline shaping by introducing one filter and three reducers. The service refines incoming candidates after Resolve and derives display-ready values before the UI renders the committed State.

The service registers the filter and reducers, and the component renders the committed display-ready State. That separation makes it clear why filtering, sorting, and display derivation belong in the pipeline instead of inside the template.
